basics.simple: A slice of ownership in a company.
basics.deep: You own a claim on future profits. Price = what others will pay for that claim today.

basics.simple: An organization that turns inputs into products people pay for.
basics.deep: Its value is the cash it can return to owners over its whole life.
The market's price tag on the whole company. Compare companies by market cap, never by share price.

basics.simple: Money customers pay — the top line.
basics.deep: Growth in revenue matters only if it eventually becomes profit.
Gross → operating → net profit, each removing more costs.
Buybacks raise EPS without the business growing — check both.
What you pay per $1 of profit. A 25 P/E means a 4% earnings yield.

basics.simple: Cash from operations minus capital spending.
basics.deep: The cash that can actually be returned to owners. Harder to manipulate than earnings.

basics.simple: Borrowed money with fixed claims ahead of shareholders.
basics.deep: Debt amplifies outcomes. In a downturn, lenders get paid first — shareholders can be wiped out.

basics.simple: Profit as a share of revenue.
basics.deep: High and stable margins usually signal pricing power.

basics.simple: Operating profit after tax ÷ capital invested.
basics.deep: The single best quality measure: how much profit each dollar reinvested earns. ROIC above cost of capital (~8–10%) creates value.

basics.simple: What you pay relative to what you get.
basics.deep: Great company + bad price can be a bad investment. Expected return = yield + growth ± change in multiple.
Growth is worth more when ROIC is high and runway long.

basics.simple: A durable advantage that keeps competitors out.
basics.deep: Sources: network effects, switching costs, scale, brands, patents, regulation.

basics.simple: Doing something rivals can't easily copy.
basics.deep: Moats are the long-lived version; advantages can be temporary.

basics.simple: An event that can make the market change its mind.
basics.deep: Earnings, products, regulation, spin-offs. Catalysts put a clock on a thesis.

basics.simple: The chance of permanent loss — not just volatility.
basics.deep: Volatility is the price of admission; permanent loss is what to avoid.

basics.simple: Owning things that don't fail together.
basics.deep: 10 AI stocks are one bet. Correlation, not count, is what matters.
A 20% chance of 5× and 80% chance of −50% has EV +20% — but you may not survive the losses. Size for survival.

styles.name: Value investing
styles.why: Investors overreact to bad news; mean reversion in fundamentals and multiples.
styles.when: After panics; when rates fall; when cheap stocks are not value traps.
styles.fails: Value traps; technology disruption; long periods (2010–2020) when growth dominates.
styles.risk: Paying a low price for a declining business.

styles.name: Growth investing
styles.what: Own companies growing fast for a long time.
styles.why: Compounding of revenue and profit outruns any starting valuation.
styles.fails: Rising rates; growth decelerates while priced for perfection (2000, 2022).

styles.name: Quality investing
styles.why: Markets underprice persistence of high profitability.
styles.fails: Junk rallies; when quality becomes expensive.

styles.name: Momentum
styles.why: Under-reaction to news, herding, slow capital flows.
styles.fails: Sharp reversals after bear-market bottoms (2009 momentum crash).

styles.name: Factor investing
styles.what: Systematically tilt toward rewarded traits (value, momentum, quality, size, low vol).
styles.why: Risk premia or persistent behavioral errors.
styles.when: Over long horizons, diversified across factors.
styles.fails: Factors can underperform for a decade; crowding.

styles.name: Contrarian
styles.fails: When the bad news is correct.

styles.name: Special situations
styles.why: Forced sellers and complexity create mispricing.

styles.name: Event-driven
styles.what: Trade around defined events (earnings, approvals, deals).

styles.name: Long-term compounding
styles.why: Time × ROIC × reinvestment; low taxes and costs.
styles.fails: If you sell in panics or the moat erodes.

styles.name: Thematic
styles.what: Invest in a structural trend (AI, electrification).

styles.name: Macro
styles.what: Position based on rates, inflation, growth, currencies.
styles.fails: Macro is hard to forecast and timing is everything.

styles.name: Optionality
styles.what: Small positions with large possible payoffs.

quant.deep: Simple return r = P1/P0 − 1. Multiply (1+r) across periods to compound.
They add across time, which makes math easier. ≈ simple return for small moves.
Monthly σ × √12, daily σ × √252. The S&P 500 has run ≈15–16% per year since 1900.

quant.simple: How two return streams move together (−1 to 1).
quant.deep: Diversification works when correlations are low — and they rise in crises.
Drives portfolio variance: σp² = wᵀΣw.
Cross-sectional (winners vs losers) and time-series (asset vs its own past).
Works at short horizons in some assets; FLOW's index test failed out of sample.

quant.simple: Average of the last N prices.
quant.deep: A slow average is a crude trend detector. Price above = trend up.
Rotate toward stronger assets.
β = cov(r, m)/var(m). β 1.5 moves ~1.5× the market.

quant.simple: Return not explained by market exposure.
quant.deep: Most 'alpha' disappears after costs and correct benchmarks.

quant.simple: Common drivers of returns across stocks.
quant.deep: Market, size, value, momentum, quality, low volatility.
(R − Rf)/σ. 0.5 ≈ stock market long-run; >1 sustained is rare.
Only penalizes bad volatility.
The number that decides whether you'll actually stick with a strategy. S&P 1929–32: −81%.

quant.simple: Bet on relationships between many securities converging.
quant.deep: Needs low costs, fast execution, and leverage — institutional territory.

quant.simple: Long one, short a related one when the spread widens.
quant.deep: Requires short selling (account permissions). Relationships break.

quant.simple: Persistent states: bull/bear, high/low vol, inflation up/down.
quant.deep: Strategies that work in one regime often fail in another.
Necessary, never sufficient.
Test many ideas → the best one is lucky. Use out-of-sample data and simple rules.

quant.simple: Using information not available at the time.
quant.deep: Example: trading on a month's close at that month's start. FLOW shifts all signals one period.
Today's index members excluded the failures — inflates returns.
FLOW charges 10 bps/switch (index) and 5 bps/side (swing).

quant.simple: Getting a worse price than the signal price.
quant.deep: Grows with size and volatility.

quant.simple: How much to put in each trade.
quant.deep: Risk per trade (e.g., 1% of capital) ÷ distance to stop = position size.

swing.simple: Holding positions for days to weeks to capture a 'swing' in price.
2 days – 8 weeks. Long enough to avoid intraday noise, short enough for frequent decisions.
Higher highs and higher lows. Trade with it — the base rate is on your side.
Speed of the move. Strong momentum tends to persist briefly, then fade.
Price zones where buying or selling previously overwhelmed the other side.
Participation. Breakouts on heavy volume are more credible (not testable in FLOW's data).
Price leaves a range. Most fail; the few that work run far — low win rate, high payoff.
Temporary dips inside an uptrend. High win rate, small wins — vulnerable to regime shifts.
Wider stops in volatile markets; smaller size to keep risk constant.
Gaps around earnings can jump stops — reduce size or avoid holding through.
Most stocks follow the index. Fighting a falling market lowers win rates.
Target at least 2:1 reward-to-risk, or a high win rate if lower.
Decide before entry what price proves you wrong.
Risk 0.5–1% of the paper account per trade.
Losing streaks of 6–10 trades happen even with an edge. Size so they're survivable.

trading_styles.name: Day trading (concepts)
trading_styles.fails: Most retail day traders lose money after costs; US pattern-day-trader rules require $25K margin accounts.

trading_styles.name: Trend following
trading_styles.idea: Own what's rising, exit what's falling.

extreme_upside.needs: Revenue +50–70% with flat multiple, or steady growth + modest re-rating. Achievable for quality growth.
Revenue roughly doubles AND margins expand or multiple rises. Requires a real inflection.
Revenue 3× plus profitability inflection; usually a small/mid cap (<$30B) at the start.
A new market or category win: revenue 5–10× AND a re-rating. Base rates are low; most candidates fall 70%+ along the way.

upside_math: Return multiple = (Revenue_end/Revenue_start) × (Margin_end/Margin_start) × (Multiple_end/Multiple_start) × (Shares_start/Shares_end). Every 10× needs several of these to move at once.
